title: The Hammer, the Chair, and the Poet Seen From Behind: a Rhinelander Made Swiss
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Mannheim, the Theatre and the Physician of Mainz

stops.name: Mannheim, the birth in the Kurpfalz
stops.date_confidence: contradicted, not resolved: en and de Wikipedia give 7 September 1795, and the existing atlas file carl_jung_of_mainz carries that date; fr Wikipedia gives 7 June 1794; Deutsche Biographie (GND 130921572, citing NDB 10 (1974) p. 677) and the Basler Professorengalerie catalogue give 1794-1864. Day-precision exists only for 1795; the scholarly apparatus favours 1794.
stops.campa: A son is born to Franz Ignaz Jung, Catholic physician of Mainz, and to Sophie Ziegler his wife, in a Mannheim that belongs this year to the Electoral Palatinate and will belong to Baden before the boy is ten. The armies of the First Coalition and of Revolutionary France are working the Rhine over, and the father is away with a field hospital in that fighting. The child is entered as Carl Gustav. Which year the register holds, 1794 or 1795, is a thing the family never settles, and the catalogues of Basel are still disagreeing with the encyclopaedias about it.
sources: Deutsche Biographie, GND 130921572, citing NDB 10 (1974) p. 677
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of the Jesuitenkirche, Mannheim, searched in the 1950s and found to hold no support for the Goethe tradition

stops.name: Mainz, the father's city
stops.date_confidence: undated: the Mainz origin is a standing family fact rather than an event, and no source places the elder Jung himself in the city; the year here is a placeholder anchored to his birth
stops.campa: Mainz carries the name before Mannheim needs it. Franz Ignaz Jung, born 1759, keeps a Catholic practice in this city, and behind him the household tells of Dr Carl Jung of Mainz, a physician of the seventeenth century from whom the line is said to run. No document puts the newborn of Mannheim in these streets. The city is an origin, not a visit. What comes down from here is the trade, and the older physician attached to it by telling rather than by paper. Franz Ignaz Jung dies in 1831.
suggested_refs: The Mainz physicians' registers of the eighteenth century, in which the Jung practice would be entered

stops.name: Mannheim, the theatre and Sophie Ziegler
stops.date_confidence: undated tradition: MDR's editorial footnote places Sophie Ziegler and her sister in the Mannheim Theater circle without dates; the placeholder is anchored to the birth year and sits before the September birth date
stops.campa: Sophie Ziegler and her sister move in the circle of the Mannheim Theater and are friends of writers who pass through it. That is the whole of what the family later agrees on. Out of the theatre and its visitors grows the other story, the one told in Basel drawing rooms and repeated at the professor's own table: that one of those writers was Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, and that the child of 1794 or 1795 was his. The baptismal register of the Jesuitenkirche at Mannheim is searched for it in the 1950s, by an editor working on the grandson's book, and holds nothing.
stops.quote: The wife of my great-grandfather (Franz Ignaz Jung, d. 1831), Sophie Zegler, and her sister were associated with the Mannheim Theater and were friends of many writers. The story goes that Sophie Zegler had an illegitimate child by Goethe, and that this child was my grandfather, Carl Gustav Jung.
stops.quote_source: C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ed. Aniela Jaffe, trans. Richard and Clara Winston (Pantheon, 1963), footnote to the 'School Years' chapter
sources: C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections (1963), 'School Years' footnote
Deirdre Bair, Jung: A Biography (Little, Brown, 2003), ch. 1
suggested_refs: The Mannheim National Theatre and its literary circle in the 1790s

stops.name: Heidelberg, coming up to read medicine
stops.date_confidence: unknown: fr.wikipedia records the Heidelberg study without a matriculation year, and no reachable register gives one; the placeholder sits three years before the attested 1816 doctorate
stops.campa: He comes up the Neckar to Heidelberg to read medicine. The university stands in the Grabengasse behind the old town, small, Protestant, and full of students who have come back from the war with a nation in their heads and no country to put it in. He arrives a Catholic doctor's son out of the Palatinate, and not yet twenty. No matriculation year survives in any register a later reader can reach. That he studied here is attested; the year he began is not recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: The Alte Universitat, Grabengasse 1, Heidelberg

stops.name: Heidelberg, the conversion and the Burschenschaft Teutonia
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1815 by en.wikipedia; month and day not given
stops.campa: He leaves the church he was baptised in. The liberal and nationalist talk of the student rooms takes him first and the confession follows the politics: he goes over to Protestantism, and he joins Teutonia, one of the Burschenschaften sworn to a Germany that does not exist. He is twenty. The fraternities keep membership lists and are proud of them, and within four years the Prussian police will be reading those same lists as a register of suspects. The year of all this is given as 1815; the month is not.
suggested_refs: The Burschenschaft Teutonia at Heidelberg and the fraternity colours of the post-1815 student movement

stops.name: Heidelberg, De evolutione corporis humani
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en, de and fr Wikipedia and by Bair; month and day not given
stops.campa: He takes the doctorate in medicine and in the natural sciences, summa cum laude, on a dissertation called De evolutione corporis humani, the development of the human body. He is twenty-one, or twenty-two, according to which birth year one credits. The subject he picks is the body assembling itself out of nothing recognisable into a man. He keeps it for the rest of his working life. Of the dissertation itself, the later record carries the title and the grade and nothing more.
stops.quote: graduating summa cum laude with a doctorate in medicine and the natural sciences, awarded for a dissertation entitled 'De evolutione corporis humani.'
stops.quote_source: Deirdre Bair, Jung: A Biography (Little, Brown, 2003), chapter on family origins
suggested_refs: De evolutione corporis humani (Heidelberg, 1816), not consulted for this file

stops.name: Jena, the students gather
stops.date_confidence: attested as preceding the Wartburg journey in the same year; no day given by any reachable source
stops.campa: The Burschenschaften call their men to Jena, the seat of the first of them, and the young doctor goes. They come in from Heidelberg, Giessen, Halle and Erlangen, walking or riding, carrying black, red and gold cloth that no state on the map recognises. What is settled at Jena is that they will go on together to the Wartburg for the tercentenary of the Reformation. He is a graduate among undergraduates, five hundred miles from the Rhine, going north-west across Thuringia in the autumn with the rest.
suggested_refs: The Urburschenschaft of Jena, founded 1815

stops.name: Weimar, the poet seen from behind
stops.date_confidence: undated: the grandson reports the sighting from the elder Jung's diaries without a year; placing it beside the 1817 Thuringian journey is inference, not attestation
stops.campa: He is in Weimar in these years and sees Goethe. He writes it in his diary and writes nothing else about him: no meeting, no word exchanged, no claim. The poet is seen from behind, in the street, once. Basel will say openly, later, that this man is Goethe's son, and this man will not correct Basel. The diaries he keeps every day of his adult life hold that one line, with no date attached to it. His grandson goes through them and finds no more, and prints the sentence in a footnote.
stops.quote: My grandfather says not a word about it in his diaries, however. He mentions only that he once saw Goethe in Weimar, and then merely from behind!
stops.quote_source: C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ed. Aniela Jaffe (Pantheon, 1963), footnote to the 'School Years' chapter
sources: C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections (1963)
goethe_full.journey.json (this atlas, absence check: no mention of Jung)
suggested_refs: Goethe's residence at the Frauenplan, Weimar

stops.name: Wartburg, the festival of the tercentenary
stops.date_confidence: attested: de.wikipedia gives the Wartburgfest as 18-19 October 1817
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of October, three hundred years after the theses and four years after Leipzig, the students climb to the Wartburg above Eisenach, where Luther hid and translated. There are speeches, a torch procession, a bonfire into which reactionary books are thrown. The German princes take note of every face that can be named to them. Carl Gustav Jung, doctor of medicine, aged twenty-two or twenty-three, is one of the faces on the hill. The gates of the castle are shut behind the last of them at dusk.
suggested_refs: The Wartburg above Eisenach and the festival of 18-19 October 1817

segments.name: Berlin: the Charite and the Hausvogtei

stops.name: Berlin, assistant to Johann Nepomuk Rust
stops.date_confidence: inferred: no source gives a year, so the stop is placed between the 1816 doctorate and the 1819 arrest; Bair's 'when only twenty-four' is itself hostage to the disputed birth year
stops.campa: Berlin, and the Charite, where Johann Nepomuk Rust runs the surgical and ophthalmic service and takes his assistants young. Jung comes to him for the eye and the knife, the two crafts that will make a man employable in any city in Europe. It is the ordinary next step for a good graduate, and it puts him in the Prussian capital a year before Prussia begins reading fraternity membership lists as registers of suspects. Bair puts him at twenty-four when the call comes, an age hostage to a birth year nobody has settled.
stops.quote: when only twenty-four, he was called to Berlin to become surgical assistant to the legendary Charite Hospital ophthalmologist, Johann Nepomuk Rust
stops.quote_source: Deirdre Bair, Jung: A Biography (Little, Brown, 2003)
suggested_refs: The Charite, Berlin, and the surgical service of Johann Nepomuk Rust

stops.name: Berlin, the hammer that Sand gave him
stops.date_confidence: the assassination is attested to 23 March 1819; the date of Jung's own arrest is not given by any reachable source, and the stop is set on the day the crackdown begins
stops.campa: Karl Ludwig Sand, Burschenschafter and friend of Jung's, walks into the house of the playwright August von Kotzebue and stabs him dead for a Russian agent and a mocker of the students. Prussia answers with decrees and with arrests. In Jung's rooms they find a hammer, the short kind used for splitting rock, which Sand had given him. That is the whole of the evidence against him, and it is enough. The court convicts, and the sentence is thirteen months.
stops.quote: Carl Gustav I, whose crime was mere possession of the kind of hammer used in mineralogical research, a gift to him from Sand, was imprisoned for thirteen months in Hansvogtai prison.
stops.quote_source: Deirdre Bair, Jung: A Biography (Little, Brown, 2003); 'Hansvogtai' is a garbling of the Berlin Hausvogtei
suggested_refs: The Carlsbad Decrees of 1819 and the Prussian proceedings against the Burschenschaften

stops.name: Berlin, thirteen months in the Hausvogtei
stops.date_confidence: the thirteen-month sentence is attested; its start and end dates are not recorded in any reachable source, so the stop is set across the middle of the term
stops.campa: The Hausvogtei on its own square is the royal court prison of Berlin, and it holds him thirteen months. He is not a conspirator and the state does not pretend that he is one. He is a young doctor who kept a friend's hammer. He comes out while the crackdown is still hardening, unemployable in Prussia and a convicted man in every German state that shares the lists. Everything he builds after this, he builds outside Germany. The month of his release is not recorded.
suggested_refs: The Hausvogtei on Hausvogteiplatz, Berlin, the royal court prison

stops.name: Paris, looking for a laboratory
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1821 by en and de Wikipedia; month and day not given
stops.campa: He goes to Paris and looks for a place in research. The city is the medical capital of the age, its hospitals full of clinicians teaching at the bedside, and full also of Germans who have left home for the reason he has left home. Nothing comes of it. He is twenty-six or twenty-seven, with a Heidelberg doctorate, Rust's training, and a conviction on his record, and no Paris laboratory opens to him. The next year he crosses to Basel instead. Where he lodged in Paris, and on whose money, he does not record.
suggested_refs: The Paris clinical school of the 1820s

segments.name: Basel: the Chair, the Bones, the Rectorate

stops.name: Basel, the appointment at the Rheinsprung
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1822 by fr.wikipedia and by carl_jung_of_mainz.journey.json; month and day not given
stops.campa: Basel takes him. The university is old, small, short of teachers in the medical sciences, and seated since 1460 in the house above the Rheinsprung, where it will stay until 1939. He is appointed to the faculty and given surgery, anatomy and obstetrics, which in a faculty this size is most of what a physician needs to know. He is a foreigner and a convert, with a Prussian conviction behind him and no German post open to him. He will hold a chair in this city for forty-two years.
suggested_refs: The old University of Basel at Rheinsprung 9, its seat from 1460 until the Kollegienhaus opened in 1939

stops.name: Basel, the pamphlet with a question for a title
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1823 by en.wikipedia; month and day not given
stops.campa: His first full year of teaching produces a pamphlet with a question for a title: whether Basel can found the institutions medical study most needs. The answer inside is that it cannot, not as things stand, and that the city will have to build them. He is one year into the post, telling a conservative republic of guilds and merchants what its university lacks. Basel does not throw him out for it. Within a year it makes him a citizen. He is twenty-eight, and he has been in the country eighteen months.
suggested_refs: Konnen in Basel die nothigsten Hulfsanstalten zur Forderung medizinischer Studien gegrundet werden? (Basel, 1823), not consulted for this file

stops.name: Basel, the anatomical collection begun
stops.date_confidence: the 1824 founding is attested by de.wikipedia, 'Anatomisches Museum Basel'; the coordinate is the museum's present home in an institute opened in 1921, because the site of his own theatre is not established in any reachable source
stops.campa: He begins the anatomical collection: preparations, specimens, bone, the working stock a teacher of anatomy needs and Basel has never assembled. It becomes the anatomical museum of the university and outlives every building it is kept in, moving at last into an institute opened in 1921, fifty-seven years after his death. Where he first housed it, no reachable record says; the theatre he taught in has left no address. Students are still taught from the collection.
suggested_refs: The Anatomisches Museum Basel, Pestalozzistrasse 20, founded as a teaching collection in 1824

stops.name: Basel, made a citizen of the republic
stops.date_confidence: the year 1824 is attested by en and de Wikipedia; the month and day of the grant are not recorded in reachable sources
stops.campa: The republic makes him a citizen of Basel, grants him the freedom of the city, and with it he takes Swiss nationality. He is thirty, and no longer the subject of any German prince who holds his name on a list. He holds assistant professorships in surgery, anatomy and midwifery. The Jung family becomes Swiss on this day, which is why every Jung after him is born in Switzerland and speaks of Germany as a place other people come from. The grant goes into the register of the republic under his name.
suggested_refs: The Basel grant of Burgerrecht, 1824

stops.name: Basel, rector, and the address on anatomy
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1828 by en.wikipedia and corroborated by carl_jung_of_mainz.journey.json; the research pool's geography lens wrongly reported the rectorate as undatable
stops.campa: Six years after arriving he is installed rector of the University of Basel, and takes for his rectoral address the relation of anatomy to medical science: that the discipline the city treats as a preliminary is the ground of the whole art. As rector he pushes through reforms and sets up charitable foundations. The German states still hold a convict of 1819 on their lists. Basel holds a rector. The address goes to the printer that year, and the reforms he pushes through are not itemised anywhere reachable.
suggested_refs: Uber das Verhaltniss der Anatomie zu der medicinischen Wissenschaft (Basel, 1828), his rectoral address

stops.name: Basel, a drama signed Demius
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1831 by en.wikipedia; month and day not given
stops.campa: A drama in three acts, Die Revolution, comes out under the name Demius. The author is the professor of anatomy. It is 1831, the year after Paris rose again and the year the Swiss cantons are rewriting their constitutions, and a Basel professor who once wore the fraternity colours does not sign such a thing with the name on his lecture list. What stands in the play, nobody in the family afterwards appears to have read closely enough to report. The pseudonym holds. The city never publicly puts his name to it.
suggested_refs: Die Revolution: Originaldrama in drei Akten (1831), published under the pseudonym Demius, not consulted for this file

stops.name: Basel, the hospital moved into the Markgraflerhof
stops.date_confidence: the 1842 move of the Burgerspital is attested by de.wikipedia; fr.wikipedia credits Jung with renovating the civic hospital without a date, and the identification of the two is a reconstruction
stops.campa: The Burgerspital moves into the Markgraflerhof on the Hebelstrasse, three hundred and twenty-two beds, the city's hospital now tied to the university that teaches inside it. He has a hand in the rebuilding: the French account credits him with renovating the civic hospital without saying when, and this is the year the hospital changes. For the first time his students can be walked from the dissection room to a living ward and back in a morning. He is forty-eight in the year the beds are carried across the city.
suggested_refs: The Markgraflerhof on Hebelstrasse, seat of the Basel civic hospital from 1842

segments.name: The House, the Wives, the Thirteen

stops.name: Basel, three wives and thirteen children
stops.date_confidence: undated: en.wikipedia names the three wives and at least thirteen children but gives no marriage years and no order of the marriages; the placeholder sits in the middle of his Basel decades
stops.campa: He marries three times: Virginie de Lassaulx, Elisabeth Reyenthaler, Sophie Frey. He fathers at least thirteen children. In what order the wives came, which of them bore which child, and when each marriage was made, nothing reachable records. What does survive is the temper of the house. His son Ernst calls him severe, a ruthless disciplinarian; the biographer who prints that phrase adds, in her own voice and outside the quotation marks, that his children were eager to leave.
stops.quote_source: Ernst Jung, his son, quoted in Deirdre Bair, Jung: A Biography (Little, Brown, 2003), p. 13
sources: Deirdre Bair, Jung: A Biography (2003), p. 13
suggested_refs: Basel marriage registers of the 1820s to 1850s, which would settle the order of the three marriages

stops.name: Basel, the son who took up drawing instead
stops.date_confidence: undated reconstruction: en and de Wikipedia name Ernst Georg Jung as his son and an architect but give no birth year; the placeholder sits in his father's middle Basel years
stops.campa: One son, Ernst Georg, does not take the scalpel. He becomes an architect, in a city rebuilding its hospital and its university rooms inside his working life. When he was born, and to which of the three wives, is not established anywhere a later reader can check, and no building of his is named in any reachable source. He is the son who leaves the four words about his father's household that everyone since has quoted: severe, a ruthless disciplinarian.
sources: Deirdre Bair, Jung: A Biography (2003), p. 13
suggested_refs: Basel building registers of the mid-nineteenth century, for the works of Ernst Georg Jung

stops.name: Basel, the youngest son born
stops.date_confidence: the birth year 1842 is attested by en.wikipedia, 'Carl Jung'; the day, the house, and which of the three wives was his mother are gaps
stops.campa: The youngest son is born and named Johann Paul Achilles Jung. He will not be a physician either. He goes to theology, takes a country parish, and ends as pastor at Kleinhuningen on the poor edge of Basel, a man of small means in a family of professors. Through him the name passes on, and the legend with it. Which of the three wives is his mother, no reachable source answers; the house in Basel where he was born is not recorded. They christen him Johann Paul Achilles, and the family calls him Paul.
suggested_refs: Basel baptismal registers for 1842, which would name Paul Achilles Jung's mother

stops.name: Basel, the two accounts of the same man
stops.date_confidence: undated: Bair gives no year for either characterization or for the health diaries; the placeholder sits in his late middle years
stops.campa: Two accounts of him run side by side in the record and are never reconciled. In the house he is the disciplinarian his children hurry away from. In the city, late, he is a man of irresistible charm, kind-hearted, tactful and humorous, the professor Basel came round to. In his own hand there is a third account, and where it is now Bair does not say: meticulous diaries of his health, persistent coughing, frequent fever, nausea, indigestion, depression.
stops.quote: a man of irresistible charm, kind-hearted, tactful, and humorous.
stops.quote_source: A characterization current in Basel, quoted by Deirdre Bair, Jung: A Biography (Little, Brown, 2003), p. 12
sources: Deirdre Bair, Jung: A Biography (2003), pp. 12-13
suggested_refs: The elder Jung's health diaries, described by Bair; present whereabouts unstated in reachable sources

segments.name: The Brain Papers and the Institute of Hope

stops.name: Basel, the eminence in the ventricle
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1843 by en.wikipedia; month and day not given
stops.campa: He publishes on the lateral eminence in the lateral ventricle of the human brain: a short paper about a swelling in a cavity, of the kind an anatomist writes when he has been opening the same structure for twenty years and finds it undescribed. He is nearly fifty and has taught in Basel since he was twenty-seven. The brain is the part of the body he comes to last. The paper survives in the bibliographies as a title, Uber die seitliche Erhabenheit in dem Lateral-Ventrikel des menschlichen Gehirnes, 1843.
suggested_refs: Uber die seitliche Erhabenheit in dem Lateral-Ventrikel des menschlichen Gehirnes (1843), not consulted for this file

stops.name: Basel, the vault of the brain
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1845 by en.wikipedia; month and day not given
stops.campa: Two years on, the vault of the human brain: the arch of white matter under the great commissure, one structure, named and drawn. He is fifty-one, a professor of anatomy who has spent a career showing what the body is by cutting it open carefully enough to see it. The specimens go into the collection he founded. The students are walked past them. His grandson is born thirty years after this paper, and will spend his own life on the same organ approached from the other side.
suggested_refs: Uber das Gewolbe in dem menschlichen Gehirne (1845), not consulted for this file

stops.name: Basel, the article he did not sign
stops.date_confidence: undated: Bair gives neither title, journal nor year for the anonymously printed article, placing it only among his prolific years; the placeholder sits in the middle of them
stops.campa: Somewhere in these years, printed without his name on it, he puts a proposal to the medical public. Not an asylum of the usual sort. An institute that would take in the sick of every kind and attempt their cure by psychological means, attached, he suggests indirectly and discreetly, to a medical university. Basel is conservative in the extreme and he does not sign. Neither the title of the article nor its journal nor its year is recorded. What survives is one sentence, quoted by Bair in 2003.
stops.quote: I am not thinking of a lunatic asylum of the usual sort, but of an institute that would admit ill people of all kinds, whose cure could be attempted by means of psychological treatment.
stops.quote_source: Carl Gustav Jung the elder, anonymously printed article, quoted in Deirdre Bair, Jung: A Biography (Little, Brown, 2003), p. 12
sources: Deirdre Bair, Jung: A Biography (2003), p. 12
suggested_refs: The anonymous article on psychological treatment, title and journal unidentified: an open bibliographic question

stops.name: Basel, the chair of internal medicine
stops.date_confidence: contradicted: en and de Wikipedia give the chair as 1855-1864; fr.wikipedia says he taught internal medicine from 1854. Not resolved
stops.campa: He becomes the first full professor of internal medicine at Basel, setting down the surgery and anatomy he has taught for more than thirty years and taking up the treatment of the body whole. He is sixty, and it is the last post he takes. He holds the chair until he dies in it. Even the year he takes it up is disputed: the German and English records say 1855, the French record has him teaching internal medicine already in 1854, and nothing reachable settles between them.
suggested_refs: The Basel chair of internal medicine, first held 1854 or 1855

stops.name: Basel, the founding of Zur Hoffnung
stops.date_confidence: the founding and the year 1857 are attested by fr.wikipedia; the site within Basel is not established in any reachable source
stops.campa: He founds Zur Hoffnung, Hope, a house for children with mental disabilities: the ones no Basel school will take and no hospital treats. It is the proposal of the unsigned article built at the smallest scale a private man can manage, not an asylum but an institution that admits and attempts. Where in the city it stood, nothing reachable records. He is past sixty when he opens it, and has seven years left. What became of the house after his death is not recorded in any reachable source.
suggested_refs: Zur Hoffnung, Basel, founded 1857 for children with mental disabilities; site unidentified

stops.name: Basel, master of Friendship and Constancy
stops.date_confidence: undated: fr.wikipedia records the office without a year, so the placeholder is set before the 1844 union of the cantonal lodges; no reachable source gives the lodge house's address, so the pin is the old university quarter rather than a located building
stops.campa: He is made venerable master of Zur Freundschaft und Bestandigkeit, Friendship and Constancy, the Basel lodge founded in 1808. Freemasonry in these decades is where the liberal professions of a conservative city meet one another outside their guilds: doctors, lawyers, merchants who read. He came to the lodge as he came to everything else here, a foreigner made citizen. In which house the lodge met, and in which year he took the chair, no reachable source records.
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Karl Gustav Jung', citing Le Guide du Franc-Macon (Groupe de Recherche Alpina, 1998)
suggested_refs: The Basel lodge Zur Freundschaft und Bestandigkeit, founded 1808; meeting house unidentified

stops.name: Switzerland, the cantonal lodges united
stops.date_confidence: the 1844 founding is attested by fr and de Wikipedia; neither names a founding city, so the pin is the Swiss centroid rather than a located place
stops.campa: The cantonal lodges of Switzerland unite into one national body, the Grande Loge Suisse Alpina. Its first grand orator is Jonas Furrer, who four years later becomes the first president of the Swiss Confederation. The young federal state and the young grand lodge are made in the same decade by overlapping men, and the Basel professor of anatomy stands inside both. In which city the founding was held, no record reachable now says. The lodges bring their charters and their separate rites into one obedience.
suggested_refs: The founding of the Grande Loge Suisse Alpina, 1844; founding city unrecorded in reachable sources

stops.name: Switzerland, elected Grand Master of the Alpina
stops.date_confidence: the 1850 election as second Grand Master is attested by fr and de Wikipedia and by Bair; the pool's 'Basel, civic seat of the Alpina Grand Mastership' is an invented location and is not used
stops.campa: He is elected second Grand Master of the Alpina and holds the office alongside his Basel chair. A man convicted in Berlin in 1819 is now the senior officer of a Swiss national institution and a professor of the university of the city that naturalised him. He is fifty-five, or fifty-six, on the two datings of his birth. The lodges of the whole confederation elect him, not his own at Basel. Bair reads the election as a measure of how far the name had carried by then.
stops.quote: In 1850, he was so prominent throughout Switzerland that he was elected Grand Master of the United Swiss Freemasons societies.
stops.quote_source: Deirdre Bair, Jung: A Biography (Little, Brown, 2003)
suggested_refs: The Grand Mastership of the Grande Loge Suisse Alpina, 1850-1856

stops.name: Switzerland, the grand mastership laid down
stops.date_confidence: the 1856 end of the six-year tenure is attested by fr.wikipedia; month and day not given
stops.campa: Six years, and the grand mastership passes to another man. He is sixty-one and lets go of the last of the offices that are not medicine, keeping the chair and the collection and the house for children. Where the Alpina's grand master sat in those years, at Basel or anywhere else, the record does not say. The office travelled with whoever held it, and now it travels away from him. The Alpina keeps his name second on its list of grand masters, after one man and before all the rest.
suggested_refs: Alpina grand-mastership succession lists, 1856

segments.name: The Grave, and the Grandson Who Carried the Name

stops.name: Basel, death in the chair of internal medicine
stops.date_confidence: the date and place of death are attested by en, de and fr Wikipedia and by Deutsche Biographie; his age is not, since the birth year is disputed: sixty-eight on the 1795 dating, seventy on the 1794
stops.campa: He dies at Basel on the twelfth of June, holding the chair of internal medicine, forty-two years after he crossed into the city with a Prussian conviction and no post. Whether he is sixty-eight at that moment or seventy depends on which birth year is credited, and the sources have never agreed: the Basel professors' catalogue, which holds his portrait, prints 1794 to 1864, while the German and English encyclopaedias print 1795. He is buried in the week that follows.
suggested_refs: Basel death register, 12 June 1864

stops.name: Basel, laid in the Wolfgottesacker
stops.date_confidence: burial at the Wolfgottesacker is attested by en and fr Wikipedia; the day of interment is not recorded in reachable sources and is set here to the day of death
stops.campa: The Wolfgottesacker lies east of the old city, out past the goods yard, and he is put into it. Nothing about the grave marks him as other than a Basel professor. The Goethe story goes into the ground with him and comes straight back out again: his sons repeat it, his grandson repeats it to schoolfellows, an editor a century later checks the Frankfurt archive and the Mannheim register and finds nothing, and the story goes on being told anyway. The cemetery is still out there, between the goods yard and the tram depot.
suggested_refs: The Wolfgottesacker cemetery, eastern Basel

stops.name: Kesswil, the grandson given the name
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia, 'Carl Jung', and jung.journey.json in this atlas
stops.campa: Eleven years after the funeral a son is born to the pastor Paul Jung and to Emilie Preiswerk in the parsonage at Kesswil above the Bodensee, and they name him Carl Gustav after his grandfather. The child takes the name, the profession his father declined, and the legend, all three at once and without being asked. Carl Gustav Jung will carry them for eighty-six years and hand the last of them on in stone. The parish register enters the birth on the twenty-sixth of July.
suggested_refs: The parsonage at Kesswil, Thurgau, birthplace of the psychiatrist

stops.name: Basel, the bust by Ferdinand Schloth
stops.date_confidence: the commission is attested to 1876 and the relocation to 2008 by en and de Wikipedia; the pin is the Skulpturhalle, where the bust has stood since 2008, not its original site
stops.campa: Basel commissions a bust of him from the sculptor Ferdinand Schloth, twelve years after the funeral. It is the only public monument the city gives him. In 2008 it is carried into the Skulpturhalle and set down among the plaster casts, so that the Rhinelander who taught Basel its anatomy now stands in the same room as copies of gods and emperors, labelled with two dates that the museums of his own city cannot agree on. Schloth works from portraits, twelve years after the face he is cutting was last seen in the street.
suggested_refs: The Schloth bust of Karl Gustav Jung, Skulpturhalle Basel since 2008

stops.name: Kleinhuningen, the story told in the parsonage
stops.date_confidence: undated reconstruction: the household's telling of the legend during the grandson's childhood is inferred from Memories, Dreams, Reflections, which records only that he first heard it from strangers
stops.campa: In the parsonage at Kleinhuningen, on the river edge of Basel where the barges tie up, Paul Jung's household keeps the grandfather going as a story. The pastor is poor, his marriage is unhappy, and his father was a rector, a grand master, and a man Basel said was Goethe's son. The boy hears it at home and hears it from strangers in the town, and cannot afterwards say which of the two came first. The barges come up the Rhine past the garden wall. It is the last poor parish the family will hold.
sources: C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections (1963)
suggested_refs: The Kleinhuningen parsonage, Basel, still standing

stops.name: Basel, the grandson matriculates in medicine
stops.date_confidence: the year 1895 is attested by en.wikipedia; the precise day appears only in the existing atlas file jung.journey.json and could not be corroborated in any external source
stops.campa: The grandson matriculates in medicine at the University of Basel, in the faculty his grandfather led as rector and taught in for four decades. He picks up the scalpel his father put down. He entertains his fellow students with the family legend: the illegitimate son of Goethe, the great-grandmother in the Mannheim theatre. Later he pulls back from it and says only that Sophie Ziegler was a friend of Goethe's niece. The day of his matriculation is given as the eighteenth of April, in one record only.
stops.quote: I think not, however, for I know that I first heard this tale from strangers. I should add that there is an annoying tradition that my grandfather was a natural son of Goethe.
stops.quote_source: C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections, ed. Aniela Jaffe (Pantheon, 1963)
suggested_refs: The University of Basel medical faculty register, 1895

stops.name: Basel, the portrait in the professors' gallery
stops.date_confidence: undated: de.wikipedia catalogues the portrait as A 40, Abb. 109 with life dates 1794-1864 but gives no year for the painting or for its hanging; the placeholder is a round year after his death
stops.campa: His portrait hangs in the Basel professors' gallery, in the aula of the museum on the Augustinergasse, catalogued A 40, plate 109, Karl Gustav Jung, 1794 to 1864. That catalogue is one reason the birth year cannot be settled: it prints 1794 without hesitation against the encyclopaedias that print 1795, and it is the city's own record of its own professor. Who painted it, and when, the catalogue does not say. He looks out of the frame in the gown of the office he held in 1828.
suggested_refs: The Basler Professorengalerie in the aula of the Museum an der Augustinergasse, entry A 40, Abb. 109

stops.name: Weimar, the congress in the poet's town
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the congress date comes from jung.journey.json in this atlas, and the resonance with the family legend is noted by biographers rather than stated at the congress itself
stops.campa: The Third International Psychoanalytical Congress meets at Weimar, and the grandson comes to it at the head of the movement. It is Goethe's town, and the men around him know the family story. His grandfather had been here once and wrote in his diary that he saw the poet, from behind, and wrote nothing more. The photograph taken at the congress puts him in the front row of it. Whether he thought about his grandfather that week, nothing he wrote at the time says.
sources: C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections (1963)
suggested_refs: The Weimar congress photograph, September 1911

stops.name: Bollingen, the tablets cut in stone
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the date and the wording of the tablets come from jung.journey.json in this atlas, citing Memories, Dreams, Reflections
stops.campa: At the tower he built himself on the upper lake, in the year he loses his wife, the old psychiatrist cuts memorial tablets for the ancestors of the House of Jung. One of them is for the Basel doctor, the legend-line of Goethe. What began as talk among theatre friends in Mannheim, and passed through a professor who enjoyed telling it, is now chiselled into a wall by a man of eighty who has stopped arguing with it. He cuts the letters himself, in the stone of a tower that has no electricity in it.
sources: C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections (1963)
suggested_refs: The ancestral tablets at the Bollingen Tower, Lake Zurich

stops.name: Kusnacht, the legend and its disproof on one page
stops.date_confidence: the recollections were dictated across the grandson's last years and published in 1962; no single date attaches to the passage on his grandfather
stops.campa: In the house on the lake at Kusnacht, at the end of his life, the grandson dictates his recollections and the family legend gets its last hearing. He calls the tradition annoying and says he first heard it from strangers. His editor goes and checks: the Goethehaus archive at Frankfurt, the baptismal register of the Jesuitenkirche at Mannheim, and prints in a footnote that no proof was found. The book goes out to the world with the story and the disproof on the same page.
stops.quote: No proof of this item of family tradition has been found in the available sources, the archives of the Goethehaus in Frankfurt am Main and the baptismal register in the Jesuitenkirche in Mannheim.
stops.quote_source: Aniela Jaffe, editorial footnote in C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections, trans. Richard and Clara Winston (Pantheon, 1963)
sources: C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections (1963), 'School Years' footnotes
suggested_refs: Memories, Dreams, Reflections (1962), and the Goethehaus archive at Frankfurt
